figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: What one model run costs (Qwen3.5-2B on an M2 Pro). A run over 8 tokens costs $1.6\times$ a run over one, not $8\times$, because the run is dominated by reading the weights. So skipping runs saves time, and tokens added to a run that happens anyway are almost free.
figures.headline: A run over 8 tokens costs 1.6 times a run over one token, not 8 times, on the 2B model on an M2 Pro.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Left: the smallest graph with two walks between a pair; it is 2-strongly few. Right: a vertex with one way in and one way out is forced: whoever enters a forced chain walks it to its end. Theorem 11 says that once forced chains are contracted, at most $2k$ vertices remain between any two vertices; in decoding, a forced chain is output the model is not asked about.
figures.headline: The smallest graph with two walks between a pair is shown, and after forced chains are contracted at most 2k vertices remain.
citing_sentences: Fig. 2 shows the two shapes that recur below: two walks between a pair, and a forced chain.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The step graph. Left: an automaton for a quoted word. Middle: part of the vocabulary trie. Right: their product from $q_{1}$. Every trie node appears with the one state the automaton is in when it gets there, so there is exactly one route to every vertex. The token "a is dead from $q_{1}$ because no letter may follow the closing quote.
figures.headline: The step graph gives exactly one route to every vertex, because each vocabulary trie node appears with one automaton state.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: One constrained output, token by token (Qwen3.5-2B, the person schema). White: sampled by the model (27 tokens, 27 passes). Blue: forced by the constraint (7 tokens, fed in the passes of the preceding sampled tokens). The key splits (name then ":") are the tokenizer’s own (Section C.4).
figures.headline: Of one constrained output, 27 tokens are sampled in 27 passes and 7 tokens are forced inside those passes.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: A recursive schema as an automaton with a stack. A child node is a “call”: the engine pushes the place to return to ($r$) and starts a new node; the node’s closing bracket pops it. The whole state, stack included, is a small integer vector on the GPU.
figures.headline: A recursive schema runs as an automaton with a stack: child nodes push a return point and closing brackets pop it.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Certified parallel decoding. The fields of a JSON object are drafted at the same time, as rows of one batch, then the model checks the whole draft in one run. The result is identical to decoding token by token.
figures.headline: Drafting the fields of a JSON object in parallel and verifying them in one run gives output identical to token-by-token decoding.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: A server that receives sixteen different grammars (Qwen3.5-4B). With token tables, memory grows by hundreds of megabytes per grammar, the fourteenth grammar waits 26 s for its first answer, and the fifteenth crashes the server. With stcon, all sixteen fit in about 1 GB and first answers stay fast.
figures.headline: With token tables the fifteenth grammar crashes the server, while the recomputed-mask engine fits all sixteen in about 1 GB.
citing_sentences: When a server sees many different grammars, as an agent platform does, tables accumulate until the process crashes; ours serves all sixteen within about 1 GB (Table 10, Fig. 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Practical results in two numbers. Left: one request at a time, same model and kernels, $1.28\times$ faster than llguidance’s fast-forward mode and $1.77\times$ faster than its mask-only mode, with the same answers. Right: the whole engine on an agent workload, $2.55\times$ faster than the baseline, stock mlx-lm with llguidance.
figures.headline: The engine is 1.28 times faster than llguidance fast-forward on one request and 2.55 times faster on the agent workload.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: The all-state pass, level by level (person schema, 104 states). Gray: trie nodes of the 248k-token vocabulary by byte depth. Blue: rows Algorithm 4 keeps alive at that level (a row dies only when it is dead for all states). Depths beyond 20 hold under 1% of the nodes.
figures.headline: Trie nodes alive per depth in the all-state pass fall quickly, and depths beyond 20 hold under 1% of the nodes.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: What a wider pass costs (Qwen3.5-2B, one stream). A pass over $S$ tokens costs far less than $S$ passes, because it is bound by reading the weights. On the 4B a pass costs 13 ms at $S=1$, 21 ms at $S=4$ and 39 ms at $S=16$.
figures.headline: On the 4B, one pass over 16 tokens takes 39 ms, against 13 ms for one token, so wider passes are cheap.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Left: decode speed against context length (2B, one stream, 128 output tokens). Right: batched constrained serving (2B, 18 JSON extraction jobs, best of two runs, all outputs valid). With the schema in the prompt our drip engine is $1.33\times$ and $1.31\times$ faster than mlx-lm’s batch generator with llguidance at 4 and 8 slots and level at 16, where a step is bound by arithmetic and forced spans buy nothing on a uniform batch. The compact hint puts only keys and enum options in the prompt (118 instead of 212 tokens) and lets forced spans supply the syntax: $1.5$–$1.6\times$ at every slot count.
figures.headline: Batched JSON serving is 1.33 and 1.31 times faster at 4 and 8 slots, and 1.5–1.6 times faster with compact hints.

figures.caption: Validity against the token budget (Qwen3.5-2B; budget as a fraction of each task’s full answer; six regular and four recursive tasks). Without the mask every cut output is invalid. With it, outputs shorten gracefully; where the masked regular curve is below 100%, the budget is below the shortest valid answer for some schemas.

figures.caption: The budget mask on one output. As the budget tightens the decoder closes the array early, then shortens strings, then empties them, because it admits only tokens after which a valid ending still fits.

abstract: Language models are more and more often asked for structured output: JSON that follows a schema, or a tool call with typed arguments. A small machine, an automaton, enforces the format by forbidding the tokens that would break it. We observe that this machine has a rare property: from any of its states, each token leads along exactly one path. Graphs in which only a few paths join any two points are a classical object of complexity theory, and our theoretical result settles an open question about them: one can decide whether such a graph connects two points while verifying that it really has few paths, with very little memory. Precisely, the problem lies in the classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, and needs only $O(\log^{2}n/\log\log n)$ space, below the classical $O(\log^{2}n)$ of Savitch’s theorem. The constructions behind the proofs become an inference engine: text the format forces is written without running the model, the mask is recomputed on the GPU without any table, recursive formats use a small stack, every output stays valid under a token limit, and independent fields are decoded in parallel and verified. On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B, against MLX with llguidance, the standard setup for this hardware, schema-constrained extraction finishes $1.2$–$1.3\times$ sooner with the same answers, a grammar costs 3 MB instead of up to 1.5 GB, one server holds sixteen grammars where tables run out of memory, and sixteen tool-calling agents finish $2.5\times$ sooner.

sections.body: The paper starts from one property: a token read from a state of a format automaton leads to exactly one next state, so the reachable graph is a tree. Such few-path graphs are a classical topic in complexity theory. The paper answers an open question of Apers and Edenhofer: deciding reachability while verifying few paths needs logarithmic memory and lies in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, with space $O(\log^{2}n/\log\log n)$. The same constructions drive a decoding engine on MLX. On one Apple M2 Pro (16 GB) with Qwen3.5-2B, six JSON extractions take 1.89 s against 2.41 s for MLX with llguidance, and sixteen tool-calling agents take 29.3 s against 74.6 s.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Constrained decoding adds per-step cost on a laptop, and this paper links it to a complexity question about few-path graphs.

sections.body: This section fixes the terms. A laptop decode step is dominated by reading all the weights, so a run over several tokens costs little more than a run over one, and tokens that can be written without a run save a whole run. A JSON schema compiles to a deterministic automaton over bytes with a few hundred states. A graph is k-strongly few if at most k walks join any two vertices, and a mangrove if at most one does. Such a graph has no cycle. A forced chain is a run of vertices with one way in and one way out. Table 2 lists the classes, with directed reachability as the benchmark whose best known deterministic bound is Savitch's $O(\log^{2}n)$.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: A laptop run is dominated by reading weights, and few-path graphs are defined as those with at most k walks between vertices.

sections.body: The problem STCONsf asks, for a graph, two vertices and a bound k, whether the graph is k-strongly few and whether t can be reached from s. The algorithm is not promised a good graph, so it must also reject graphs with cycles or exponentially many walks, in the same small memory. The first idea stops every search at a budget of nk walk lengths, which forces termination even on cyclic graphs. The second gives each walk a polynomial hash, certifies that no two walks collide, and then counts. The third uses the product of the terms (N-0) through (N-k), which is zero exactly when the walk count N is at most k; summing squares of these products gives one zero test. Further results cover budgets, compilers and a threshold where binary k gives PL-completeness.
sections.heading: The theory in plain words
sections.headline: Three ideas (budgets, certified fingerprints, one zero test) show total few-path reachability lies in ReachUL and related classes.

sections.body: The vocabulary is stored as a trie, and each automaton state is paired with every trie node. This gives a step graph that is a tree, so every token has one path. Six mechanisms follow, each proved in Appendix C. The mask is recomputed on the GPU at each step in 7 to 18 microseconds, against a 7 to 15 ms model run, instead of a table of up to 1.5 GB. A grammar then costs its automaton plus 2.9 MB of shared vocabulary. Forced text is fed in the same model run as the preceding sampled token, and it uses the tokenizer's own split. A budget rule with shortest-path tables keeps outputs valid under any feasible limit. Recursive formats use a GPU stack capped at 64 entries, and independent JSON fields are drafted in parallel and then verified.
sections.heading: From the theory to the decoding engine
sections.headline: The decoding step graph is a tree, which yields six mechanisms for masks, forced text, budgets and parallel fields.

sections.body: Experiments run on one Apple M2 Pro with 16 GB, using Qwen3.5-2B and 4B in 4-bit precision with greedy decoding. The baseline is MLX with llguidance, run inside the same decode loop. On six JSON extractions the 2B takes 1.89 s against 2.41 s for llguidance in its best mode, and the 4B takes 3.89 s against 4.59 s. The gain has two parts: 226 model runs instead of 343, and 8.3 ms per run instead of 9.7 ms. On the 2B the outputs of the two engines are character for character identical. Every timing is a median over interleaved rounds on one machine.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Six JSON extractions take 1.89 s on the 2B model against 2.41 s for MLX with llguidance, with the same answers.

sections.body: Few-path complexity work includes Buntrock, Jenner, Lange and Rossmanith, who introduced unambiguous few-path logspace computation, and Allender and Lange, who introduced mangroves and the simulation of ReachUL. Apers and Edenhofer solved few-path reachability in quantum logspace and asked for its classical complexity. For constrained decoding, Outlines precomputes allowed tokens per state, llguidance computes masks on the CPU with fast-forward tokens, and XGrammar and SynCode handle context-free grammars. SGLang decodes runs of forced transitions in one step. Speculative decoding and lookahead decoding verify drafts; the paper says its forced spans are drafts accepted with certainty.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Related work covers few-path complexity results and constrained-decoding libraries, and speculative decoding.

sections.body: The gains come from two sources that do not depend on hardware. Skipping model runs for forced text helps wherever a run is expensive relative to the constraint. Keeping the mask on the GPU helps wherever the CPU and GPU would otherwise take turns. When a server batches many requests so that each step is limited by arithmetic, the first gain shrinks; at 16 slots it disappears, while the memory gains remain. The stated limitations are one machine and one model family, six JSON schemas, four recursive schemas, greedy decoding, a recursive path that serves one request at a time, and certified parallel decoding that saves model runs but not yet wall time on this GPU.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The paper expects the gains on memory-bound devices, but tests cover one machine, one model family and greedy decoding.

sections.body: The conclusion restates both halves. Total few-path reachability, the question of Apers and Edenhofer, is solved with logarithmic memory by an unambiguous machine, by a deterministic stack machine and by a single zero test, in less memory than Savitch's bound. The same constructions organize structured decoding. Forced text costs no model run, the mask is recomputed instead of stored, forced text keeps the tokenizer's split, recursion uses a small stack, outputs stay valid under any feasible limit, and independent fields run in parallel and are verified. The summary is that few paths mean fast decoding.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that the same constructions settle few-path reachability and make structured decoding cheaper.

sections.body: This is a priority statement. It says the theoretical results, including the placement of total few-path reachability in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2 and the budget, threshold and structure results, were obtained independently by the author in August 2026. It says the remaining time went to the practical application: identifying the few-path structure of constrained decoding, deriving the mechanisms and their guarantees from the proofs, and building the engine on MLX. The section is an authorship claim and gives no separate measurement.
sections.heading: Statement of novelty
sections.headline: The author states the theory was obtained independently and the remaining time went to the practical engine.

sections.body: The appendix is organized by topic. Appendix A explains decoding, caches, constraints and streams in plain words, and lists what goes wrong on a laptop: tables of 77 MB to 1.5 GB per grammar, a server that fails at the fifteenth distinct grammar on the 4B, and host-side masks that cost a step's worth of time. Appendix B gives the formal statements and proofs of Section 3, and Appendix C those of Section 4. Appendix D describes the engine as implemented. Appendices E to H hold the measurements, Appendix I the negative results, such as sibling-parallel decoding that fails, and Appendix J the exactness checks and the automated tests.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers background, formal theory and proofs, the implementation, all measurements, negative results and tests.
